comprehensive.reason: Port injection surface for React tree.
The adapter — only file allowed to import the vendor; profile names storage/refresh/claim/token-type mechanics load-bearing here.
Single-flight refresh helper — the owned-behavior nucleus for Axis 2.
Authorization decisions — the sole call site the design intends for Axis 4.
API client — 401/refresh/failure path and the injection call site.
App-layer component — proves the boundary is actually used.
App-layer component — verifies authz reads go through the policy, not claims.
App-layer page — verifies domain-Principal reads only.

findings.statement: Vendor imports from aws-amplify are confined to the single adapter file src/auth/adapters/cognito.ts; no other application-layer file imports the vendor.
findings.note: A repo-wide grep for aws-amplify / amazon-cognito / fetchAuthSession / AuthSession / AuthUser / setKeyValueStorage returns hits only inside the adapter and inside the mocks in __tests__/auth-contract.test.ts — the latter is expected (the contract test intentionally stubs the vendor at the import boundary).

findings.statement: No vendor types (AuthSession, AuthTokens, JWT, AuthUser, FetchUserAttributesOutput, Amplify AuthError) appear as parameter types, return types, or exported types in application-layer code outside the adapter.
checked_patterns: Amplify AuthError (distinct from the domain AuthError defined in src/auth/types.ts)
findings.note: Domain AuthError is defined in src/auth/types.ts as a local class — it is not the vendor's error and does not constitute a leak.

findings.statement: An AuthPort-shaped contract exists — the boundary the app depends on.
The API client receives the AuthPort by injection, not by importing a vendor singleton.
AuthProvider injects an AuthPort instance into React context; components read domain Principal via useAuth() without touching the vendor.
A conformance suite is written against AuthPort and runs against both a FakeAuth and the real CognitoAuthAdapter — the migration-readiness signal for B3.
findings.note: Assertions target the domain shape only (see line 76: expect(key.startsWith("cognito:")).toBe(false)); the vendor is mocked at the import boundary rather than being asserted on.

findings.statement: No server-rendered auth surface exists in this codebase: no SSR adapter imports, no createServerRunner / runWithAmplifyServerContext, and no client-vs-server branching to obtain auth.
checked_patterns: typeof window branching to select an auth path
findings.note: React-only client app (react@18 declared; no next / Nuxt / SSR runtime declared). The client/server split does not arise here, so B4 is not applicable rather than absent.

findings.statement: Token storage is a custom adapter implementing KeyValueStorageInterface, plugged into the v6 storage seam via cognitoUserPoolsTokenProvider.setKeyValueStorage — not the vendor default localStorage and not a built-in selector.
findings.note: This is a user-defined class implementing the interface, not a built-in selector (defaultStorage / sessionStorage / new CookieStorage()) — the look-alike distinction the profile calls out. Caveat from the profile: setKeyValueStorage overrides the TokenStore only; if Cognito Identity Pools were in use, identityId would remain in localStorage. Identity Pool usage was NOT detected in this codebase, so that caveat does not currently apply.

findings.statement: No Amplify v5 storage-configuration patterns appear (the codebase is confirmed v6 by package.json).
checked_patterns: Amplify.configure({ Auth: { cookieStorage: { domain, path, expires, ... } } }) — v5 built-in selector
Amplify.configure({ Auth: { storage: <class> } }) — v5 custom storage class
findings.note: Recorded to satisfy the playbook's rule that a storage claim under Amplify must be checked against BOTH v5 and v6 patterns.

findings.statement: A single-flight refresh helper deduplicates N concurrent 401s into a single refresh call.
The API client owns the 401 path: on 401 it calls onRefresh, retries once on success, and routes to onSessionExpired on failure — reactive, single-flight, with an explicit failure route.
The adapter's onRefresh drives refresh through the single-flight helper using fetchAuthSession({ forceRefresh: true }) — refresh is explicit, not inherited vendor magic.

evidence.quote: const session = await fetchAuthSession({ forceRefresh: true });

findings.statement: An explicit session-expired failure route exists on the port and is invoked from the 401 path.
Cognito-specific claim names (cognito:groups, custom:tenantId) appear only inside the adapter's getPrincipal, where they are mapped into a domain Principal.
No inline reads of vendor claim shapes or vendor-namespaced features appear in application-layer code.
checked_patterns: cognito: (namespaced claim access — cognito:groups, cognito:username, etc.)
hard-coded role/group string literals matched against claim reads

findings.statement: Outbound API calls are authorized with the access token, not the ID token — the profile's hardening recommendation for Cognito apps is already met.

Authorization decisions run through a single policy function taking a domain Principal — the boundary produces a Principal (with domain roles), and can(principal, action) is the sole authorization site.

evidence.quote: export function can(principal: Principal | null, action: Action): boolean {

findings.statement: Application components call the policy function rather than reading claim/role strings inline.

b1_anti_corruption.note: Vendor imports and vendor types confined to the adapter; no leak into components, pages, or API code.

b2_injected.note: AuthPort interface exists and is threaded via a factory (createApiClient) and React context — no module-level vendor singleton is imported by app code.

b3_contract_tested.note: runAuthContractTests asserts against the domain shape and runs against both FakeAuth and the real CognitoAuthAdapter — migration = new adapter that passes this suite.

b4_client_server_split.note: React-only client app; no SSR surface (no Next.js / adapter-nextjs / server-import path). The concern does not arise here.

cognito.note: MemoryKeyValueStorage implements KeyValueStorageInterface and is plugged into cognitoUserPoolsTokenProvider.setKeyValueStorage — a user-defined class, not a built-in selector. Storage in this codebase is swappable at one call site.

storage.recommended_seam: Custom KeyValueStorageInterface implementation passed to cognitoUserPoolsTokenProvider.setKeyValueStorage — already in place. A move to HttpOnly cookies would replace the MemoryKeyValueStorage class body without changing any call site.

cost_evidence.basis: The v6 storage seam is already taken by a custom adapter at src/auth/adapters/cognito.ts:32; retrofit to a different storage backend is confined to swapping the MemoryKeyValueStorage class inside the adapter file (single file, no call-site changes).

cognito.note: Reactive 401-interceptor with single-flight dedup and an explicit onSessionExpired failure path. The adapter forces refresh via fetchAuthSession({ forceRefresh: true }) rather than relying on Amplify's silent-refresh magic.

refresh.recommended_seam: 401 interceptor in the injected API client → auth.onRefresh() (single-flight) → retry once → auth.onSessionExpired() on failure. Already in place at src/api/client.ts and src/auth/refresh.ts.

cost_evidence.basis: Refresh is already owned: the helper (src/auth/refresh.ts:6), the 401 path (src/api/client.ts:19), and the explicit expiry route (src/auth/adapters/cognito.ts:71) are in place. Moving to a different refresh strategy (e.g. HttpOnly-cookie server refresh) changes the adapter's onRefresh body and does not require altering call sites.

cognito.note: Cognito-specific surface (cognito:groups, custom:tenantId, aws-amplify imports, setKeyValueStorage) appears only in src/auth/adapters/cognito.ts. The rest of the app speaks the domain shapes defined in src/auth/types.ts.

identity_provider.recommended_seam: Provider-specific behavior confined to one adapter file that implements AuthPort. A provider swap = write a sibling adapter (e.g. Auth0) that passes runAuthContractTests. Already the shape here.

cost_evidence.basis: Vendor imports and claim names are localized to a single file (src/auth/adapters/cognito.ts). Coupling spread outside the adapter = zero confirmed hits across src/components/**, src/pages/**, src/api/**, and the remaining src/auth/** files. Swap = one new adapter + green contract suite.

cognito.note: Domain Principal is mapped once (in the adapter's getPrincipal), then the sole authorization site is can(principal, action) in src/auth/policy.ts. Components ask the policy; they do not read claim shapes. API calls attach the access token (not the ID token) — the profile's Cognito-hardening default is met.

authorization.recommended_seam: The boundary produces a domain Principal; a single policy function is the only authorization decision site; API calls carry the access token. All in place.

cost_evidence.basis: Authorization decisions run through one function (src/auth/policy.ts:13); zero inline claim reads confirmed across app layer; access token is already the API bearer. Moving to RBAC/ABAC or adding finer permissions edits the Principal shape and src/auth/policy.ts — no call-site sweep required.

judgment_calls.question: Is a token storage change actually on the table (e.g., HttpOnly cookies, encrypted store, session cookies)?
judgment_calls.context: The seam already exists (custom KeyValueStorageInterface adapter plugged in at src/auth/adapters/cognito.ts:32), so a storage change stays inside that file. Whether it is worth doing now depends on the roadmap, which the code cannot see.

judgment_calls.question: Is owning refresh (or any other vendor-owned runtime behavior — sign-out propagation, multi-tab sync, silent re-auth) on the roadmap independently, or would it move only alongside a storage change?
judgment_calls.context: Refresh, single-flight dedup, and the explicit expiry route are already owned in this codebase. Sign-out cross-tab propagation via Amplify Hub is not wired — this is a deliberate design choice or a deferred item; only the maintainer knows which.

judgment_calls.question: Is a provider swap realistic in the next 12–24 months, and how much vendor-specific behavior (Cognito groups, custom attributes) is acceptable to keep?
judgment_calls.context: The current shape localizes vendor-specific surface to a single adapter file, so a swap = one new adapter passing runAuthContractTests. Whether that's actually going to happen — or whether the defensive optionality is worth continued investment — is a roadmap call.

judgment_calls.question: Are authorization-model changes planned (RBAC/ABAC, finer-grained permissions), and are any backend contracts assuming the current token/role shape?
judgment_calls.context: Access tokens already authorize the backend and one policy function is the only authorization site — the two calcification traps this axis catches are already avoided. Any evolution stays local to src/auth/policy.ts and the Principal shape, but whether the backend will accept those shapes is not visible in this repo.

judgment_calls.question: What is the true retrofit cost in your team's context (bandwidth, test coverage beyond the shipped contract suite, adjacent services that depend on the current shape)?
judgment_calls.context: The mechanical cost read on every axis is 'low' because the seams are in place; that is not the same as 'cheap in your calendar.' Real time-to-complete is yours to state.

synthesis.posture: well-bounded; near migration-ready across all four axes

headline.text: The boundary is fully in place: aws-amplify imports, Cognito claim names, and the storage seam live only inside src/auth/adapters/cognito.ts; a runAuthContractTests suite in __tests__/auth-contract.test.ts:50 exercises the port against both a FakeAuth and the real CognitoAuthAdapter; refresh is owned (single-flight + explicit onSessionExpired); API calls carry the access token; and authorization decisions run through a domain Principal + can(principal, action) policy function. In migration-readiness terms this codebase is essentially at 'swap provider = new adapter that passes the contract suite' — the remaining calls are the maintainer's to make.
